@@8578372 <h> TheBull PREMIUM <p> Trends <p> &amp; <p> Opportunities <h> Is King Coal on Life Support ? <p> By Bob Kohut 02.05.2016 <p> On 27 April a story appearing here on thebull.com reported the sad tale of the " last train to leave Leigh Creek . " The train carried coal from a now-shuttered mine in the town formerly operated by electricity retailer Alinta Energy for the South Australian state government . At its peak the mine produced about 2.5 million tonnes of coal per year to fire two power generating stations that supplied 40% of South Australia 's electricity . Coal mining at Leigh Creek dates back to 1888 . <p> Since the advent of electricity , coal has been viewed as the " king " of commodities . But even with the most highly valued commodities , technology can issue a death sentence . More than a century ago the world had a seemingly insatiable demand for whale oil to light the night . The onset of kerosene sent whale oil demand plummeting , leaving only its use in soap and vegetable and certain machine oils @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ whaling fleet left the Port of New Bedford Massachusetts in 1921 . <p> The future of coal is a hotly debated topic . There are those who firmly believe thermal coal used to generate electricity will join whale oil as an obsolescent commodity as natural gas and renewable energies become dominant . Like or not , coal is a " dirty " fuel , pouring carbon into the atmosphere . <p> Metallurgical or coking coal used in the production of steel appears to have a better long term outlook , but even here steel is losing ground to lighter materials in many sectors , most notably automotive and aviation . In addition new technologies such as high-powered electric arc furnaces ( EAF ) are already used in lieu of coking coal in both the US and Europe . <p> Others scoff at the notion that King Coal is on its deathbed , believing the abundance of coal and its supposed price advantage over other forms of energy will keep coal afloat for decades to come . <p> We think the question to be addressed is not what the future of coal @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ stocks as viable investment opportunities . Coal is a major Australian export commodity , making it a prime candidate for wishful long term thinking . Investors hoping for a rebound in the price of coal can find market experts proclaiming better days ahead due to rising demand in emerging markets as well as rising prices for natural gas . <p> Despite a downward share price drift spanning more than two years , the share prices of our two largest remaining pure-play coal producers on the ASX have spiraled upward in the last month . Here is a one month price chart for New Hope Corp Limited ( NHC ) and Whitehaven Coal ( WHC ) . <p> What may have powered the move was the 16 April announcement from Indian conglomerate Adani that its proposed $21.7 billion coal mine project -- the largest new coal mine on the planet -- had received approvals from land owners in the Queensland Galilee Basin . The project faces environmental hurdles but could be serving as evidence to support the view that coal here in Australia is alive and well . <p> On 28 April @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ lower than its three month average daily volume of 218 thousand ; and Whitehaven traded 2.98 million , slightly below its average of 3.05 million . Reuters reports a consensus analyst recommendation of Hold on both stocks . Of the seventeen analysts covering the companies , only one has a Sell recommendation for Whitehaven , along with two Underperform ratings . New Hope has only one at Underperform . <p> Investors may also have been impressed with Whitehaven 's Half Year results showing a 54% increase in revenue and a return to profitability . New Hope 's Half Year results also showed a profit , albeit about half of what was reported last year . <p> Perhaps this news allowed some investors to ignore an ominous sign from the United States . On 13 April the largest coal company in the world -- Peabody Energy -- filed for bankruptcy protection in the United States . This is a company that traces its history back to 1883 when founder Francis S Peabody began selling coal from a mule-drawn wagon in Chicago . <p> King Coal believers make the case the filing is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ company 's decision to buy our own Macarthur Coal of Australia at a cost of $5.2 billion back when coal prices were high in 2011 . Management , the skeptics claim , overestimated future Chinese demand for coal and underestimated coal supplies in the Asia Pacific region . <p> There may be some truth in that explanation , but how then does one account for the August 2015 filing of the second largest producer in the US -- Alpha Natural Resources ; or the October 2015 bankruptcy of Patriot Coal ; or the January 11 bankruptcy filing of yet another major US coal producer -- Arch Coal ? The US has seen more than three dozen coal miners declare bankruptcy in the last three years . <p> King Coal believers have an answer for that as well , pointing to the explosion in US production of natural gas from shale drilling . The price of gas dropped so low it obliterated the cost advantage coal had held for decades . <p> The situation for coal miners in the US is so precarious major financial institutions there are refusing to fund any @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ including JP Morgan Chase , Morgan Stanley , Citigroup , Bank of America , and Wells Fargo . The following graph presents the apocalyptic case for coal , assuming a continuation of low natural gas prices . <p> The next graph makes the case that natural gas prices outside the US give coal an edge , especially when you factor in the increased imports of coal from the US due to the low price there driving down the price of coal in Europe . <p> The case for the future of coal here in Australia rests with China and India . For the retail investor the task of sorting through conflicting points of view is challenging at best . Here is a graph showing Chinese coal consumption in decline since 2002 . <p> Now here is another graph supporting the case for future coal demand . <p> In January of 2016 the Chinese government banned the building of new coal-fired generating plants for three years . A 16 April article in the Australian from Environment Editor Graham Lloyd sports the headline Coal 's future burns bright despite shift to renewable energy @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ with the intent of selling coal-generated electricity to Germany , where renewables are driven up the cost of energy . <p> India reportedly has more than 400 million people without electricity and the country appeared to be committed to coal to expand its electrical generation capability . The following graph supports that case . <p> This picture bode well for importers of thermal coal until the Indian Energy Minister very recently announced the country is planning to cut its coal imports to zero by expanding the capabilities of its state-run coal operations . <p> In 2015 Deutsche Bank issued a report appearing to support an opposite conclusion , throwing cold water on the hopes for increased imported coal . <p> We now have the Indian Energy Minister claiming solar generated electricity is already cheaper than coal but without storage capacity solar can not provide reliable 24/7 generation . <p> In the midst of all this we have confident pronouncements from the CEO of Whitehaven , with a solid Half Year financial performance in very challenging conditions to support his claim . Here is what he had to say : <p> " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ coal , particularly the outlook for the high-quality coal we produce . " <p> He went on to state the company 's financial position is expected to continue to improve over the next three years , driven by further increases in production and improving margins as well as further reductions in net debt . The strength of growth in Asian energy demand combined with production cutbacks from key exporting countries suggest that Asian coal markets will return to balance over the course of 2016 and provide the basis for a price recovery commencing in 2017 . <p> To put that into perspective we go back to 2014 when Commodity Research firm Platts named Peabody the Energy Company of the Year and its CEO the Energy CEO of the year . Here is what the CEO had to say following that award : <p> Coal will continue to dominate world energy markets for years to come . Platts ' looked at the strategy that we set out about 10 years ago to become a global player in the industry , the portfolio that we built which are the low-cost U.S. assets along @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and although Peabody will emerge from bankruptcy and continue , the shareholders will not emerge unscathed . <p> Coal is not going completely away but the ability of publicly traded coal miners to provide shareholder returns in the face of such uncertainty is questionable at best and non-existent at worst . <p> The World Coal Association ( WCA ) claims that high efficiency , low emission ( HELE ) coal-fired power plants coupled with carbon capture , use , and storage ( CCUS ) could lead to near-zero carbon emissions from coal-fired generating stations . Perhaps , perhaps not . Whatever your personal beliefs about climate change and global warming may be , everyone can agree that humans all over the planet need to breathe . @@8579061 <h> The budget must begin to repair Australia 's foreign aid program <p> Treasurer Scott Morrison addresses the media during a doorstop interview ahead of Budget day , at Parliament House in Canberra on Sunday 1 May 2016 . Photo : Alex Ellinghausen <p> When Scott Morrison made his maiden parliamentary speech in 2008 , he drew attention to the importance of foreign aid . The newly elected backbencher commended the Rudd government for its commitment to boost aid but said " we still must go further " in responding to the needs of poor communities in developing countries . " The need is not diminishing , nor can our support , " he said . " It is the Australian thing to do . " <p> Eight years on Mr Morrison , now Treasurer , is responsible for the federal budget and one of the most powerful figures in the Turnbull government . And yet his first budget on Tuesday is set to include the least generous contribution to foreign aid in our history . <p> Mr Morrison 's predecessor , Joe Hockey , slashed $11 billion @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ million is scheduled to be cut next financial year . That will reduce Australia 's foreign aid , as a proportion of gross national income , to a record low of just 0.22 per cent . The Coalition 's attack on aid spending is in stark contrast to their conservative counterparts in Britain . Despite difficult budgetary circumstances in recent years , David Cameron 's government has still managed to allocate 0.7 per cent of GNI to foreign aid . <p> The Herald urges Mr Morrison to act on the principles he expressed in his maiden speech , and at very least , not proceed with next year 's scheduled $224 million cut . Australia 's support for the world 's poorest people should not be diminishing . It is the " Australian thing " to be far more generous . <p> Advertisement <p> Last year 22 developed nations managed to increase the amount of development assistance they provided to poorer nations , according to data released this month by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development . But we went the other way . Australia and Portugal shared the dubious @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , in proportional terms , last year . After peaking at just over $5 billion in 2012-13 , Commonwealth aid spending is scheduled to fall to $3.8 billion next financial year . We 've already slumped from 13th to 16th place on the league table of wealthy donor nations , measured on a proportional basis . Experts warn we could now fall to 19th place . <p> That should be pause for thought for anyone who likes to think of Australia as a generous nation . Leaders from major church denominations last week signed an open letter calling on Mr Morrison to restore foreign aid spending . " We believe it is time to reverse course , " the letter said . " These cuts damage and undermine programs which have a direct impact on the lives , livelihoods , security and opportunity of many of our region 's poorest and most vulnerable people . " <p> Most fair-minded people agree that rich nations such as Australia have a responsibility to promote development in poorer nations . But effective foreign aid also advances the national interest , which is served by @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ one plagued by poverty . Aid has an especially important role to play in promoting stability in fragile states in our region . <p> The Australian government has delivered vital humanitarian assistance in the wake of recent extreme weather events in the Pacific region , including massive cyclones in the Philippines , Vanuatu and Fiji . These highly professional and timely emergency responses have nurtured goodwill and friendship . <p> But our region is becoming increasingly disaster-prone due to the effects of climate change . The Commonwealth is likely to be called upon more often to provide emergency aid and long-term reconstruction and development assistance as extreme weather events become more common . But experts warn the swingeing cuts to Australia 's aid program threatens to gradually denude our capacity to provide comprehensive , long-term reconstruction and development assistance following disasters . <p> A survey of 500 aid experts published by the Australian National University earlier this year found the cuts are taking a toll . Most stakeholders thought the effectiveness of Australia 's aid was worsening . That was in contrast to a similar survey in 2013 which found a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Australian aid as less effective than aid delivered by the average Western donor . Again that was a reversal from 2013 . <p> Recent cuts to Australia 's overseas aid budget have been mean-spirited . But they are also short-sighted , given the opportunities and challenges looming in our region and beyond . We know Mr Morrison values foreign aid . He and Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull should start repairing the damage in the budget .

@@8585401 <h> Budget 2016 must prepare for a post-China future <p> The era of windfall gains from a China boom has long passed and this budget may well be the last opportunity for a government to sell a coherent message about where we go from here , writes Ian Verrender . <p> For years , it was one of the most eagerly watched sports in global economics . Bets were placed and reputations staked on the one big question : When will China overtake the US to become the world 's biggest economy ? <p> Most of the time , the bets were placed on the crudest of calculations ; a straight line extrapolation of GDP growth for the two countries forever into the future . Look , it intersects on March 24 , 2017 ! <p> As far as China was concerned , there would be no downturns , no wages outbreaks , none of the problems that have beset every other nation that 's ever undergone rapid development . <p> Some economists , including the International Monetary Fund , reckon it 's already happened , about two @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ measuring . And the problem with China is , no one believes the numbers produced , let alone the calculations . As premier Li Keqiang , then just a provincial general secretary , confided to the US ambassador to China in 2007 , Chinese GDP figures were " man made " and for " general reference only " . <p> China matters a great deal to Australia . It provided a decade of unprecedented export wealth in the lead up to the financial crisis . Its massive stimulus program post 2008 propelled us into the economic stratosphere as the rest of the developed world teetered on the brink of collapse . And its performance in the next few years will determine whether this week 's budget forecasts again are a triumph of hope over reality . <p> And yet , still they continue . This week once again , we will be presented with a " credible path to surplus " . Once again , it will be based on growth forecasts that are unlikely to be attained . <p> A fortnight ago the Prime Minister , Malcolm Turnbull , returned @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ than 1000 Australians , where he praised China 's economic miracle and hailed the coming of a new dawn in trade relations between the two countries . <p> Where the mining boom is waning , as raw material supply outstrips demand from China , it is hoped agriculture and services will fill the void as the Chinese economy transitions to a consumer society . <p> There are a lot of assumptions there ; far too many to stand up to any kind of critical analysis . For a start , there are huge doubts as to whether services exports could ever topple raw materials exports . <p> Apart from tourism and maybe education , Australia has no comparative advantage for delivering financial , legal or any other services into China . Why would the Chinese , who have a proud history of civilisation extending back thousands of years , need us to provide them when they could easily do it themselves ? <p> That may explain ANZ 's recent decision to rethink its regional banking strategy , the latest in a long line of Western corporations to beat a retreat . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ economy expanded by 6.7 per cent . While that sharp deceleration was concerning , at least the numbers were bang on expectations . <p> But a funny thing happened on the way to the National Bureau of Statistics . For the first time ever , only the annual numbers were delivered . The quarterly numbers were missing . When they finally did hit the screens , after everyone had breathed a collective sigh of relief , something was terribly wrong . They did n't add up . <p> Having hitched the national bandwagon to the Chinese economy years ago , any ructions that take place there during the next few years , perhaps from its skyrocketing debt , will have a serious impact on our national income and our living standards . Do n't expect any mention of that tomorrow night . It will all be onwards and upwards . <p> It 's not just China . Last week , the US - which was supposed to be in recovery - stunned analysts when it notched up its slowest quarter of growth in two years . <p> Last year 's budget @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unrealistic growth forecasts to deliver the economy back to surplus . Mostly , it relied upon bracket creep , and a magical resurgence in growth back to trend levels of about 3.5 per cent to push workers into higher income tax levels . <p> But there are now serious questions being asked by economists about whether previous trend levels were an aberration . Could it be that the world is entering a new phase of lower growth , perhaps even stagnation ? <p> It 's not just China . Last week , the US - which was supposed to be in recovery - stunned analysts when it notched up its slowest quarter of growth in two years with a rise of just 0.5 per cent in the March quarter , almost half that of the previous quarter . <p> That was the same week Australian inflation went into reverse , into deflation , a reading that wrong-footed every forecaster and put the Reserve Bank on notice . <p> Which brings us to the budget tomorrow night . The centre-point at this stage appears to be a cut to income tax rates @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is to save middle income earners from the evils of bracket creep , the very phenomenon that just a year ago was the engine that would deliver a surplus . <p> But the proposed rejig to the thresholds tax cut has nothing to do with middle income earners . For never in history has bracket creep been less of a threat . Wages growth has all but evaporated , to the point where it has become a serious concern for policy makers . <p> The bracket shift is all about delivering a tax cut to the nation 's wealthiest . Anyone earning above $80,000 will receive a boost . And for the 400,000 Australians earning more than $180,000 , the prize will be twice as nice with the expected removal of the 2 per cent deficit levy . <p> Almost every proposal to increase revenue by closing or restricting tax loopholes , such as negative gearing , capital gains tax discounts or a serious overhaul of superannuation rorts , has been jettisoned . <p> This is not the time for pork barrel tax cuts . <p> The era of windfall gains @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ may well be the last opportunity for a government to sell a coherent message to the electorate ; to balance the books by tightening upper and middle class welfare along with expenditure restraint . That now appears unlikely . <p> Underpinning the broad cross-party support that greeted Turnbull on his ascension to Prime Minister last September was a belief that he could corral the nation into accepting some unpalatable truths about the economy and deliver us into a better future . <p> His waning popularity is a recognition that , perhaps , he 's just another politician . <p> Ian Verrender is the ABC 's business editor and writes a weekly column for The Drum . <h> Comments ( 141 ) <h> the yank : <p> 02 May 2016 7:32:35am <p> Well there is always India and Indonesia ... but seriously folks it is impossible to know what is going on in China and whether or not their economy will pull us along , best plan on it not happening any longer . <p> I find it very strange that on one side we look to China for economic growth and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ build subs to help protect us from China . <p> I do n't really think China wants to engage with others . @@8588716 <p> Financial markets are again misunderstanding or ignoring risk , and are certainly under-pricing it , both as individual institutions and systemically . The risk is another global financial crisis . <p> The GFC of 2008 had its roots in sub-prime housing loans in the United States -- simply a punt on US house prices continuing to rise - on which financial institutions built a mountain of debt instruments ( CDOs , CLOs , credit default swaps , and the like ) that were poorly understood , and certainly over-rated , and underpriced . <p> When sub-prime loans hit the wall , the mountain collapsed , many institutions failed , the whole global financial system was pushed to the brink of collapse , the global economy to a recession , and governments and policy authorities found themselves mostly rudderless , in unchartered waters . They are still struggling with an effective global response . <p> This time the risk is climate exposed investments , a risk that Hank Paulson , Secretary of the US Treasury at the time of the last GFC , has said dwarfs the risks @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of the bank of England Mark Carney has now talked openly of potential financial instability . Stopping the boats is more than some muscular rhetoric . Indefinite detention without charge or process is no empty bluff . It 's razor wire . Aimlessness . The loss of reason and despair . <p> Politics is not a game , but there is safety in numbers . <p> Safety when the numbers speak of a mute but stubborn popular consensus , a consensus that will accept self-immolation as the almost unremarkable consequence of tough-minded necessity . @@8603961 <p> A little bit of context can go a long way to understanding budget figures and policy costings . What 's the timeframe ? Is this new or recurrent funding ? Is that graph accurate ? It 's time to make the maths a bit clearer , writes Matthew Bevan . <p> Numbers are really hard , you guys . <p> I 'm one of those people who waded into year 10 maths thinking , " I 'm never going to need any of this crap ! " then waded into adult life frustrated I had n't been listening properly . <p> This week , Australian voters are going to have to do a bit more maths than usual , while they process any changes to the budget tonight , followed by the numbers-based election promises of both major parties . <p> Of the 78 promises made by the Coalition before the 2013 election being tracked by the ABC 's Fact Check , almost all of them involved a significant financial aspect , whether it was new spending , new cuts , new taxation , or just the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ election campaign will be the same . Even the legalisation of same-sex marriage , which would cost the government almost nothing to implement , now has a price tag of at least $100 million due to the expense of a proposed plebiscite . <p> So it 's up to us , the voters , to process the numbers , do our own cost/benefit analysis and make a decision at the ballot box . <p> With that in mind , I 'd like to suggest some rules for politicians and journalists to make it easier for voters to understand policies and budget measures by providing a bit more context for their numbers . <h> 1 . Give timeframes <p> Please tell me consistently whether the number you 're giving is per year , over the next four years , or between now and 2050 . When politicians and reporters describe a budget blowout , for example , whoever is in government might say the budget will be over target by $4 billion , while the opposition might say it will be over by $21 billion . <p> Both of them may be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ budget for the next financial year , while the other is describing the budget forecast over the next four years . This is confusing for your average punter who is only paying passing attention to the sound bite . <p> It can be even more confusing if you change the timeframe you refer to from one press conference to another - in one statement giving a per-annum figure and in another providing a figure projected across the forward estimates period . <p> Another issue is big projects . The $50 billion submarine build announced last week seems like a colossal amount of money . <p> It 's being touted as one of Australia 's biggest ever infrastructure projects , and one of the world 's biggest defence contracts . <p> The $50 billion might seem a little less , however , if you imagine it being spread out over a couple of decades . It only averages out at about $2.5 billion annually , assuming the last submarine comes off the slipway in 2036 . Compare this figure with the Grattan Institute 's figure on negative gearing - they say the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ policy . <h> 2 . Stop making big numbers sound small and vice versa <p> Tone really matters in statements . When you see a politician campaigning in his or her local seat , it 's amazing to see how they can make a $1.5 million spend on a local hospital sound like a bigger deal than a $1.5 billion cut to hospital funding . <p> While I 'm fully aware that at the local level a well-sold 20 grand on the roof of a leaky PCYC basketball centre can drown out coverage of a $20 million upgrade to a police station , that does n't mean journalists need to report them equally , even if one announcement comes with pictures of a minister sinking a three-point bank shot and the other comes with pictures of a boring press conference . <h> 3 . Stop the re-announcements <p> It happens all the time and both major parties do it - announcing a great funding initiative like it 's a brand new lump of spending , when it 's actually just a re-announcement of money that maybe did n't get the attention @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can also be done by announcing a big funding initiative - a $300 million environment policy , for example , then waiting a month or two to announce a specific $20 million part of it as though it 's new money . <p> For modern journalists it can be difficult to find information on what has and has n't been announced . There is n't a central register of funding announcements ( maybe there should be ) and in the rush of turning a funding announcement into a news story it 's easy to miss the fact that something identical or very similar was announced 18 months ago . <h> 4 . Provide benchmarks <p> One billion dollars is pretty meaningless for an average voter . They will never be involved with the management of that much money ( whether in a personal or commercial sense ) and it 's difficult to compare large funding announcements like that to anything they experience in day-to-day life . <p> It may be helpful for voters to compare the cost of a new announcement to a service they 're already familiar with . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ TV channels , an online TV streaming service , four national broadcast radio networks , 60 local radio stations , a multitude of digital offerings , and the most trusted news service in the country . <p> The Department of Defence turns about $32 billion a year into a high tech Army , Navy and Air Force with about 58,000 active service personnel and a large amount of hardware . <p> You can pick whatever comparison point you want , but comparing new spending or tax increases to something the public can value may assist in their understanding of the importance of any announcements . <h> 5 . Do n't put out bad charts <p> This is the most egregious of all numerical sins . It 's very , very easy to draw a chart to argue whatever you want . <p> For example , it 's easy to " prove " global warming is n't happening by having a limited date-range on your X-axis . Look ! The temperatures on this chart are going down ! Never mind the fact that the chart only shows the last five years in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ would be very easy to show a massive spike in unemployment by limiting the range of figures in your Y-axis . Look ! The line on the right is much higher than the line on the left ! Unemployment is outta control ! <p> These charts flood TV screens and Facebook timelines constantly , and they can be extremely misleading . <p> It is not always wrong to limit the range of your axes , but it is undoubtedly wrong to use the mere existence of charts to convince people of your point . <p> Now , I do n't actually expect politicians to follow any of these rules . I also doubt most of the media has the time or inclination to put announcements like these into context . <p> But when you listen to an announcement or look at a chart before making a decision as to who you 're going to vote for this year , it might be worth imagining an emotionless voice telling you about the announcement , then figure out a timeframe , try to remember if you 've heard the announcement before , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ can understand . <p> Or just vote for the leader with the better voice/suits/DJ skills/zingers/hairstyle - it is a democracy after all . <p> Matthew Bevan is a producer , reporter and newsreader for RN Breakfast . <h> Comments ( 57 ) <h> Nova4avr : <p> Thank you for this article &amp; it hits the nail right on the head . @@8604704 <h> How to rank the world 's nations by risk <p> Many of Australia 's island neighbours are vulnerable to disaster , with foreign aid playing a ' key part ' in whether national infrastructure can stand up to the challenges posed by nature . RN Breakfast reports . <p> Measuring risk on the international scale is a fiendishly complex business , but according to Matthias Garschagen , author of a report by the United Nations University in Germany , it essentially boils down to two components . <p> On the one hand , he says , is a country 's exposure to natural hazards . ' How many people are exposed to floods , to typhoons , to earthquakes ? ' <p> Not all of the immediate risks and threats that we see can be simply blamed on climate change . <p> Matthias Garschagen , United Nations University <p> On the other is the society 's inherent vulnerability . ' In other words : is the society prepared for the disaster when it strikes ? ' <p> It 's this risk matrix that explains why a nation @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ flooding -- is not estimated to be ' high risk ' . <p> ' Japan is a good example that shows a large difference between those two components , ' Garschagen says . <p> ' If you just take the exposure side , Japan would rank as one of the highest countries globally -- it 's in the comparison between the two components when you see what really needs to be done about risk . ' <p> Risky business for the Asia-Pacific region <p> The problem for many of the island nations listed in the World Risk Index is that they score highly on both sides of the ledger . <p> ' On the one hand you have natural hazards , but at the same time you also have countries with major development difficulties , ' Garschagen says . ' Hence those turn into higher base-level vulnerabilities . ' <p> In 2015 , Vanuatu was hit by Cyclone Pam , which led to the death of over a dozen people and the displacement of thousands more . <p> UNESCO estimates the cost of rebuilding will be in the hundreds of millions @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ top spot in the World Risk Report . It has occupied the top spot every year since the reports began . <p> Garschagen says the list is not designed to be predictive , but ' an event like Pam works like a validity check ' . <p> ' The risk level that we express in the index was actually matched by the very sad and tragic disaster of Pam . ' <p> ' In the long run , absolutely , but I think at the same time that not all of the immediate risks and threats that we see can be simply blamed on climate change . ' <p> For many of the larger countries in the South East Asian region , ' the homemade drivers of risk are much more extreme , and will remain so for the next few decades ' . <p> ' If you compare the rate of land subsidence due to poor groundwater extraction policies with sea level rise , you would see that . ' <p> South Pacific governments , he says , ' blame too many of their existing risks on climate change ' @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the countries on the World Risk Index are also recipients of Australian foreign aid . <p> When it comes to mitigating risk and improving adaptive capacity in developing countries , Garschagen says international assistance is key , particularly in the long term , where much of the funding goes towards risk reduction , education and public awareness . <p> ' I think in all of these domains international cooperation -- not only aid -- can play a huge role , ' he says . <p> If , as has been reported , today 's federal budget removes hundreds of millions of dollars from Australia 's foreign aid , it will be an additional stressor for programs that build risk resistance , says Garschagen . <p> ' Is the money going to flow in the mid to long term ? That 's very interesting . That 's the key question . That needs to be seen . '

@@8615569 <p> The Treasurer would like to believe his first budget is all about jobs and growth . But the only thing growing lately is the deficit and debt . And despite some admirable measures here , that 's not about to change any time soon , writes Ian Verrender . <p> It 's a well worn thoroughfare traversed by five Prime Ministers and four Treasurers in the past five years . <p> But the credible path to surplus is now in serious need of repair , cracked and chipped from repeated stumbles . Rather than being fixed , it now winds forever into the future . <p> This is a budget that banks on China continuing to muddle its way through an economic transition of monumental proportions without a hitch , paving the way for continued growth here . <p> That 's a mighty big bet . <p> If there is a fundamental failing in this document , it is that it ignores a basic tenet of mathematics ; that continually throwing away revenue is a recipe for deficits well beyond any timeframe now envisaged by the Treasury @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the planned rejuvenation of the national balance sheet are hopelessly optimistic , to the point of being unattainable . <p> Take nominal GDP . Last year it was barely hovering above the mat at just 1.6 per cent . Within two years , it 's projected to jump to 5 per cent . There 's no real explanation of how or why that will occur . <p> Nominal GDP is one of the most important measures for any Treasurer , for it incorporates value , and hence inflation . And so it is the number that determines how much money flows into the Government 's coffers . <p> It may have escaped Scott Morrison 's attention , but last week inflation lurched into reverse for the first time in eight years . It is unlikely to recover to normal levels soon . <p> That means nominal GDP is likely to lag behind real GDP , which in turn means revenue will be strangled and the deficit will expand . <p> It certainly did n't escape Glenn Stevens ' attention . As he hacked another 25 basis points off the official cash @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ feet to deliver his maiden statement , an audible intake of breath ricocheted around the halls of Parliament . <p> As the Treasurer repeated ad nauseum , this budget is all about jobs and growth . But the only proven performer in the growth stakes in the past three years has been the size of the deficit and the national debt . That 's raised the spectre of a credit rating downgrade . <p> This time last year , the deficit was forecast at $35.1 billion . By December that had blown out to $37.4 billion . Now , we 're told that we will end the financial year with a $39.9 billion shortfall . That 's a huge miscalculation in a matter of just months . <p> But still the Government refuses to countenance an increase in the tax take , instead clinging to the idea that lower taxes will lead to growth , which will then lead to more tax revenue . <p> Joe Hockey started the ball rolling when he handed out $8 billion to the Reserve Bank shortly after assuming office . Ridding the nation of the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ $6 billion a year in revenue . The carbon tax compensation , however , was kept in place . <p> It was a tradition that has been maintained . Company tax rates will decline gradually over the next 10 years , locking successive governments into either finding savings on the other side of the ledger or praying that growth magically kicks in . <p> When it comes to savings , there was a touch of ministerial chest beating about fiscal discipline since the Abbot/Hockey overthrow last September . Savings of $1.4 billion now are locked in over the next four years . <p> Divide that by four . That 's a saving of less than half a billion a year . And the deficit this year was just shy of $40 billion . It will barely scratch the surface . <p> There are some admirable measures in Scott Morrison 's first budget . Number one is the long awaited clamp down on superannuation abuse . The loophole , opened during the Howard government , that has seen Australia 's wealthiest denude Treasury of billions of dollars will be pulled tighter . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to those most in need of retirement savings ; lower income Australians and women . So no real budget relief , but an enormous shift that will partially unwind the blatant unfairness that delivers huge benefits to those with the most wealth . <p> Then there is the focus on corporate tax evasion . A new unit with 1,300 staff and beefed-up powers will operate within the Australian Tax Office to force recalcitrant multinationals to pull their weight . <p> There 's been a great deal of talk about this over the years with precious little action . Until now . <p> Within the new unit , which ATO supremo Chris Jordan will personally lead , will be 390 new recruits ; accountants , lawyers and economists , many of whom have worked for major accounting firms engaged in legal tax rorting . <p> From now on , multinationals will have to be transparent in their dealings with the ATO and co-operate . Should they fail on either count , the ATO will deem its own rate of tax . <p> Just how much this will yield is open to question @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , picking and choosing their domiciles to ensure they pay as little as possible . The action wo n't be confined to corporations either . Australia 's richest families who engage in similar behaviour will be on the radar . <p> Admirable , it may be . But it wo n't be enough to bring the budget back to balance . @@8617502 <p> Ocean acidification is causing fundamental and dangerous changes in the chemistry of the world 's oceans yet only one in five Britons has even heard of ocean acidification , let alone believes it a cause for concern . We highlighted the newspaper 's recent record of tendentious and misleading coverage of climate science ( among many other articles , it must be said , that are worthy of the paper 's name and tradition ) . <p> The " not overheating " article described a study suggesting there is no statistically valid evidence for man-made climate change -- and therefore that the planet will not warm significantly by the end of the century . But the study was not conducted by a climate scientist and it ignored basic physical laws . It did not undergo scientific peer-review and it was funded by a climate-sceptic lobby group , the Global Warming Policy Foundation . <p> The fact that a newspaper of The Times ' standing gave coverage to such a piece of research is both remarkable and deeply concerning . But it is not an isolated example . Instead it typifies a disturbing pattern in parts of the UK national media where there is an apparent determination to systematically undermine climate science and those conducting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they come with no evidence . <p> Our letter was intended to highlight the loss of credibility that inevitably comes with printing such stories . Indeed , it is precisely the failure of papers such as The Times to treat climate change properly that is prompting more informed readers to vote with their feet and turn to credible web-based news outlets such as BusinessGreen and Carbon Brief . The media is changing rapidly and established papers such as The Times are competing for readers , credibility and eventually influence against smaller publications that are often producing better coverage . <p> The Times ' loss of credibility is its own problem . However , such articles raise wider concerns about the misunderstandings generated among the public , and the loss of trust in science . <h> The media remains important <p> These problems result because , despite the proliferation of new media , the established titles continue to play a very important role in perceptions of science . They form the principal conduit through which the public and politicians access scientific information , they provide a proxy for public debate and help @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ policy-making . Thus poor-quality or slanted science reporting contributes , either unwittingly or wittingly , to the public misunderstanding of science . <p> Public misunderstanding of science can have serious consequences . In the early 1990s , The Sunday Times persisted in denying the link between HIV and AIDs after most other publications had acknowledged reality . An editorial in Nature described its reporting as " seriously mistaken , and probably disastrous " . In the late 1990s and early 2000s , media outlets gave widespread coverage to the hypothesised link between the MMR vaccine and autism -- coverage that has since been criticised as na ? ve and misleading . <p> It goes without saying that such misrepresentations of scientific knowledge run against the interests of society . People are unable to make informed decisions or to demand appropriate action from politicians . In the MMR case , outbreaks involving more than 2,000 cases of measles in 2012 were attributed to years of under-immunisation following media misreporting of the MMR issue . In the case in hand , The Times ' poor reporting on climate science has the potential to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ uncertainties in climate science , but uncertainty should not be conflated with doubt . As Naomi Oreskes and Eric Conway have so clearly documented in their excellent book Merchants of Doubt , those who wish to undermine the credibility of scientific evidence , for instance the tobacco industry in relation to cancer and smoking , have systematically tried to turn " uncertainty " into " doubt " . <p> So where does this leave us ? Editors must be free to print what they want within the law , as a free press is vital for democracy . It is entirely right that scientists , like everyone else , are subject to questioning . Not all of us are angels -- and not all research is good research . We are above neither the law nor legitimate journalistic scrutiny -- and editors are quite within their rights to seek out divergent views . <p> But the key word here is " legitimate " . Scrutiny that is carried out in the public interest with the intention of uncovering genuinely bad practice is entirely fair ; questions asked and articles slanted with @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ And even opinion articles must acknowledge the evidence , otherwise what are they but fiction ? <p> Readers also have rights -- and the right to object to distorted or biased coverage is one of them . I would argue that in the case of scientists , this extends far beyond being a right -- it is virtually an obligation . In 2014 , UK citizens invested about ? 10 billion in research and development . If research is funded by the public , then it is the public 's right to have findings disseminated accurately . And as both the recipients of public funding and the individuals with expertise in these complex subjects , the onus is on us academics to ensure that research is properly communicated . <p> Engaging with the media is not to every scientist 's taste . The journalist 's world is a lot more feisty and less respectful than ours . But in the end , accurate reporting of science matters . Editors do respond to comments and criticism . Scientists can and indeed must challenge poor reporting on climate change and , if enough @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to the benefit of scientists , the public and indeed journalism itself .

@@8625878 <h> Morrison has delivered a Menzian budget <p> Economy in transition ? Check . A focus on nation building ? Check . The politics of revenue raising ? Check ! While Scott Morrison wants us to look ahead , his first budget is very much in the style of the late great Sir Robert Menzies , writes Terry Barnes . <p> Budgets are about politics and perception , even more than economics . This election-setting budget is no exception . <p> Yet while Treasurer Scott Morrison wants us to look ahead , in many ways this budget harks back , in concept , 50 years to the prime ministership of the greatest Liberal , Sir Robert Menzies . <p> In striking ways , what Morrison laid out last night is Menzian in its conception , its nation-building goals , and its politics . <h> Conception <p> In the Menzies years Australia 's economy and society were also in transition . Today the transition , as framed by Morrison and especially Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull , is to a post-mining boom , globalised , high-tech , service-dominated economy . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ back to mining and heavy industry : farming 's share of national wealth started to decline sharply , the great wave of post-war immigration changed our Anglo-Celtic society forever , kids mostly left school at 15 , and a 1960 male baby 's life expectancy was just 67 years . <p> It was also a time of Australia becoming more prepared to look beyond Britain and the white Commonwealth for trade and wealth . <p> It was , for instance , the Country Party 's John " Black Jack " McEwen who secured the seminal Australia-Japan trade agreement of 1958 , the primitive ancestor of the major multilateral trade relationships the Abbott-Turnbull government has taken great pride in locking down . <p> Much of Turnbull and Morrison 's budget spin , with a little tweaking , could have come from Menzies and McEwen . Certainly the optimism Morrison expressed in his budget sell last night - notwithstanding un-Menzian anaemic growth forecasts and the Reserve Bank 's decision yesterday to cut interest rates to stimulate sluggish economic performance - was worthy of his golden age predecessors . <h> Nation building <p> The @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ most Liberals believed that government was a benevolent actor in economy and society , the Country Party believed in agrarian socialism , and both accepted governments protected nascent and inefficient industries from more efficient overseas competitors . <p> Morrison 's " 20-year defence industry plan " is a throwback to such notion . But it is also code for government wasting billions of scarce taxpayer dollars on constructing Australian ships , aeroplane and weapons system components , and other high-tech hardware in Australia rather than buying it more cost-effectively elsewhere . <p> The way Morrison talked about his nation-building defence industry plan last night , one could imagine the old Government Aircraft Factories producing Sabre jet fighters at Fisherman 's Bend in Melbourne or the government-owned Cockatoo Island Dockyard building British-designed destroyers in Sydney . But wait : is n't the Australian Submarine Corporation , the centrepiece of the Government 's defence shipbuilding programme , also a government business enterprise ? <p> Similar applies to the billions committed to major infrastructure projects across the nation , all needed but also carefully targeted for their maximum electoral impact . It seems every @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ almost imagine the ghost of legendary Treasury secretary Herbert " Nugget " Coombs approving the many neo-Keynesian measures in this budget , including its centrepiece Youth Jobs PaTH training programme . <h> Politics <p> Perhaps more than any other budget in recent memory , Morrison 's harked back to the Menzian political tradition of revenue-raising . If running short of revenue , raise more from taxes and borrowings , not trimming spending unless absolutely unavoidable . <p> Notwithstanding modest company tax cuts for small and medium enterprises , and bracket creep income tax adjustments for those earning between $80,000 and $87,000 , this is an old-fashioned " let 's tax more so we do n't have to cut more " budget . The lazy budgeting mentality of the 1960s has re-emerged - on both sides of politics . <p> Continuing 12.5 per cent annual hikes in tobacco excise until 2020 is a special throwback . As in Menzies ' time , smokers again are seen as cash cows carrying a disproportionate taxation burden . That , in this day and age , both Government and Opposition support raising revenue by wanting @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ disgraceful throwback to government at its laziest . <p> In the 1960s , even high-spending Coalition governments spent less than 20 per cent of Gross Domestic Product , not the whopping 25.8 per cent budgeted yesterday . For a Liberal PM and Treasurer to be proud of aiming to bring that GDP share down to a mere 25.2 per cent is something Sir Robert Menzies would deride with elegant contempt . <p> A populist Labor attack can make a plausible political case that Morrison 's company-focused and bracket creep tax cuts , and his underbidding Labor on schools and hospitals funding , do n't directly help Menzies ' " forgotten people " : workers earning less than the average wage ; unincorporated and self-employed small businesspeople ; and retirees who , between them , do so much economic heavy lifting . <p> Morrison can , and should , say his measures are n't handouts but will create more jobs , but they do n't necessarily give voters a time-honoured " what 's in it for me ? " electoral bribe in the hand . <p> Whether Morrison 's Menzian budget is @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . But it may well be that if Turnbull and Morrison recall the Menzies era , Shorten and Bowen are presiding over an Opposition nostalgic for the highly-unionised , highly-centralised , public-sector dominated world of Labor under Ben Chifley . We know how that ended in December 1949 . <p> Terry Barnes is a policy consultant , former senior Howard government adviser and weekly columnist for The Drum . It adds additional incentives . Withdraw those incentives and you slow down the escalating trend ( costs of housing ) . <p> In fact , the higher the costs of real estate the more advantageous negative gearing is . Negative gearing works in this way : You have a job that provides you @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ buy an investment property with a loan from a bank , let 's say $400,000 . You pay $24,000 p.a. in interests to the bank on that loan . You rent the property , you get $12,000 income from it . You discount the $12,000 from the $24,000 and you get a loss of -$12,000 ; you can use such loss to decrease the taxes you would pay on your $80,000 salary . <p> So , the more you borrow , the more you have to pay in interests , the more your deficit from the investment is likely to be , the more you can discount taxes on your salary .... That 's why negative gearing works better on people who are already wealthy , because they can discount higher amounts from their income in order to minimise taxes . <p> That contributes to increasing the value of real estate and therefore create bubbles .... Labor is perfectly right to target this pernicious system in order to deflate the bubble , make real estate more accessible to owners occupiers and save the country from a disastrous crash . <p> Lower @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ investor , but also helps increase the value of real estate . Photo : AP <p> Washington : As India , the world 's second-most populous country , reels from an intense drought , the World Bank has released a new report finding that the most severe impact of a changing climate will be the effect on water supplies . <p> The most startling finding ? The High and Dry : Climate Change , Water and the Economy report suggests that a lack of water could knock down economic growth in some parts of the world by as much as 6 percent of GDP by the year 2050 , " sending them into sustained negative growth . " <p> Regions facing this risk - which can at least partly be averted by better water management - include not only much of Africa as expected but @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to the report . <p> A family looks out over the mostly dry rice paddy fields near their home n Dala , Burma on Sunday . Photo : Getty Images <p> " When we look at any of the major impacts of climate change , they one way or another come through water , " said Richard Damania , a lead economist at the bank and the lead author of the report , on Tuesday . <p> Advertisement <p> Climate change hits water supplies in multiple ways . Warm temperatures can cause more evaporation of water from landscapes , while changes in precipitation can lead to both more intense individual downpours but also swings of drought conditions . <p> The threat from all this is not just to what people drink but what they eat : The human activity that consumes the most water is agriculture . <p> The dried up riverbank of the Ganges in Allahabad , India , India is reeling from a heat wave and severe drought conditions that has decimated crops , killed livestock and left at least 330 million people without enough water for their daily @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's sea-level rise . It can push into coastal aquifers , as is happening today in the state of Florida , and thus threaten to make them more saline and less usable . So it is n't only surface waters that may be depleted by climate swings , but also groundwater . <p> The World Bank report says that 1.6 billion people on Earth already live in conditions of water scarcity . Depending on the definition of the concept , other research has put that number even higher , finding that 4 billion face conditions of severe water scarcity during at least some part of the year . Either way , the World Bank fears the number will double . <p> The problem will be exacerbated by greater populations overall , and more demand for water due to increased needs in the electricity generation and agricultural sectors . <p> A man drinks water dripping from an overhead leaking pipe line in Hyderabad , India , on Monday . Photo : AP <p> " Growing populations , rising incomes , and expanding cities will converge upon a world where the demand for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ uncertain , " the report says . <p> Some of the statistics are staggering . The report finds that in the next 30 years , " the global food system will require between 40 to 50 percent more water ; municipal and industrial water demand will increase by 50 to 70 per cent ; the energy sector will see water demand increase by 85 per cent ; and the environment , already the residual claimant , may receive even less . " <p> And when water shortages happen , the poor will inevitably be hit the hardest - when it comes to both food and drinking water , because they may not be able to purchase supplies from elsewhere to get them through hard times . <p> What 's most new about the report , perhaps , is tying the problem of potential future water scarcity to dire economic impacts . " We will have expanding water deficits . When you do the analysis , it turns out that economic growth is a thirsty business , " Damania said . <p> And the problem wo n't be steady or chronic - @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ or extreme weather events , such as floods . These , again , will hit unstable regions the hardest - and take a major economic toll . <p> " When we have poverty , when we have division , when we have polarisation , you add to that a water shock , something like a drought , this becomes a threat modifier , " Damania said . <p> Ko Bo Bo collects what 's left of the water in a small pond his family uses as a water source in Dala , Burma . @@8639170 <h> Winter may be returning to Westeros , but our next ice age is on hold <h> Author <h> Disclosure statement <p> James Dyke does not work for , consult , own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article , and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond the academic appointment above . <p> The epic television series Game of Thrones makes compelling viewing for many reasons . Exotic locations and cutting edge visual effects have spectacularly translated George R R Martin 's vision onto the small screen . These production values have made the series one of the most expensive ever made and allowed the attention to detail required to build an immersive world of humans , dragons , the old gods and the new . <p> But as fantastic as this conjured world is , recent research seems to prove the old adage that fact can indeed be stranger than fiction . Because while the lands of Westeros and beyond experience dramatic shifts in weather and seasons , changes in climate here on Earth are even weirder . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ politicking and backstabbing ( not to mention front stabbing , decapitation , and immolation ) there are few constants in Game of Thrones . Long running shows typically assure us that our favourite characters will carry on and that their lives will span seasons . But anyone who has been keeping up with the Starks and Lannisters will be well aware by now that playing a central role provides no guarantee of longevity . Remember the Red Wedding ? But throughout this maelstrom there is an ever present factor . A brooding menace that belittles all the squabbles and fighting . <p> The threat of winter 's return . <p> " Oh , my sweet summer child , " Old Nan said quietly , " what do you know of fear ? Fear is for the winter , my little lord , when the snows fall a hundred feet deep and the ice wind comes howling out of the north . " <p> Winter in Westeros is a serious business . The larger towns and citadels survive with stockpiles of food and firewood . Small communities either flee or perish . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ for many years . The opening book of A Song of Ice and Fire -- A Game of Thrones from which the television series takes its name -- opens with concerns that the winter is due to return after nine years of summer . Such a long summer heralds an equally long winter . <p> Wo n't be warm for months -- or years.Sky Atlantic <p> Why the change of seasons is so unpredictable is subject of speculation in the real world and in the books . Some claim it was a consequence of a battle some 8,000 years ago . The scholars , healers , and learned men -- the Maesters -- discount this as a fable with no supporting evidence . How could humans alter the seasons ? What 's intriguing is that this Game of Thrones myth may have some basis in reality . Because something happened here on Earth about 8,000 to 12,000 years ago that could have profoundly affected the Earth 's climate and the history of all civilisations . <h> Putting the next ice age on ice <p> Glaciations , or ice ages , have @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ years , the geological period known as the Quaternary . Due to a combination of orbital mechanics , tectonic processes , and ocean currents , the Earth 's climate periodically is thrown into a reinforcing feedback loop that plunges temperatures lower and lower . The polar ice caps and glaciers expand while sea levels fall as much as 120 metres . <p> Periods between ice ages -- interglacials -- have lasted around 10,000 years in Earth 's recent geological history . Given that it 's been more than 12,000 years since the last glacial maximum , one may conclude that a new ice age is overdue . However , that may not be the case . We may have stopped it . <p> Humans began farming almost as soon as the last ice age ended . Although the numbers of humans were small , land use change such as burning fields and forests would have released carbon dioxide into the Earth 's atmosphere , which along with methane from the increased number of cattle , could have been sufficient to effectively put the next ice age on hold , so delicate @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's worth pointing out that the difference in global temperatures between our current climate and the depths of the previous glacial maximum is about 5 ? . Consider how different a world that is 5 ? warmer than today would be . <h> A long hot summer <p> A study published in the journal Nature at the start of 2016 contained the even more remarkable conclusion that human activity since the Industrial Revolution has not only paused but indefinitely delayed the series of ice ages . In fact , it may be that by elevating atmospheric carbon dioxide to levels not seen on Earth for millions of years , humans have ejected the Earth out of the Quaternary ice ages . Think about that for a moment . The process of industrialisation that began some 300 years ago has disrupted a 2.6m-year-old climate state . No more ice ages . <p> But is n't that good news ? The dawn of a new ice age would plunge civilisation into chaos . We may not have intended to , but our actions have avoided such a calamity . Unfortunately , it 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Now we fear not winter , but a period of rapid warming , the likes of which our civilisations have never experienced before . It seems unimaginable that we could effect such significant change over such a short period of time . Harder still to acknowledge is that if we are to avoid dangerous climate change , then we must radically change how we power our industrialised societies . <p> Such change will not be easy to effect . As Tyrion Lannister once observed : <p> " Most men would rather deny a hard truth than face it . " <p> An adage that could apply to some of those who wish to become the most powerful person on Earth , as much as whoever vies to sit on the Iron Throne .

@@8659048 <h> How psychology can help us solve climate change <h> Authors <h> Disclosure statement <p> Nadira Faber is affiliated with the Oxford Martin School . <p> Rachel New does not work for , consult , own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article , and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond the academic appointment above . <p> The Paris agreement on climate change calls for a global responsibility to cooperate . As we are often reminded , we urgently and drastically need to limit our use of one shared resource -- fossil fuels -- and its effect on another -- the climate . But how realistic is this goal , both for national leaders and for us ? Well , psychology may hold some answers . <p> Psychologists and economists have long explored the conflict between short-term individual and long-term collective interests when dealing with shared resources . Think of the commons dilemma : the scenario in which a field for grazing cattle works well when everyone cooperates by sticking to one cow each , but which leads to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ selfish drives take over . <p> It is useful to think about overuse of fossil fuels and its effect on the climate as a similar dilemma . If we were to think of this from a purely economic perspective , we would likely act selfishly . But psychological research should make us more optimistic about cooperation . <h> Appeal to moral sense <p> Are you more likely to overuse a shared resource when it is framed as an ethical concern or a business transaction ? Research shows people behave less selfishly when it 's framed ethically , or if we emphasise what people will gain rather than lose by reducing their use of fossil fuels . Using the phrase " global warming " rather than " climate change " also engages us emotionally and makes us more supportive of the issue . We also need a balance of good and bad news if we are not going to be overwhelmed by the enormity of the challenge and feel like running away . So wording when communicating to the public as well as in international agreements can make a difference , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ moral sense of what the right thing to do might be . <h> Reinforce social norms <p> Social norms in behaviour around climate change include things such as " most people recycle " , or " it 's not acceptable to take too many flights " . It 's been shown that communicating these norms can make people adjust their behaviour . <p> When behaviour is phrased as the default -- for example , " my neighbours do n't use too much electricity " -- people are also more likely to behave in that way , as we found in a series of experiments . <p> Research also shows that we need to believe that others sharing the resource think fairness is important if we are to act fairly , or cooperate , ourselves . So we also need a sense of shared identity , which in turn means we are more likely to think others share our values . Shared national identity could be emphasised through communication from government and media ; and at a more local level by encouraging more community involvement . <p> We also need to know @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ its capacity is . And , as we showed in recent studies , we need to know on which information we should base our behaviour and what follows from this information . So countries and local authorities being transparent about their fossil fuel usage is key and , even better , easily achieved . <h> Social beings <p> We do n't identify and act just as individuals but as members of social groups . We may belong to a family , a community , a nation and the planet , and behave in ways that benefit the group rather than the individual . A shared group identity ( such as identifying yourself as a member of your nation or the local school community ) can increase cooperation , especially if we believe that group shares our values about the environment . If you strongly identify with your community you do n't need an incentive to cooperate . <p> But at what level should this shared identity be emphasised ? Emphasising national identity can prevent cooperation between nations , by increasing competition between them . However , this can be used to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ So perhaps they could compete to be better than others at meeting climate change goals ? <p> Local competition ( like a clean city award ) can incentivise , too . But we also need to strengthen our sense of being part of the planet -- a better global identity could motivate us to empathise with other countries and even future generations . <h> Big decisions <p> Implementing the Paris agreement will involve big top-down decisions about how much each country is going to reduce their fossil fuels by . This reduction is essential to meet the goal to drastically limit the temperature increase to 2 ? C. But how should the amount of fossil fuels used in different countries be reduced when proportions vary between them ? For example , half of the remaining gas and oil reserves are in the Middle East . <p> One analysis shows that to keep the planet 's atmosphere below the target of 2 ? C , 94% of Europe 's gas reserves can be used but only 30% of those in the Middle East . Given that the Middle East has a larger @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ other countries ? Should the level of development , population or wealth of a nation also be relevant ? And what about how much fuel they have already used ? <p> Fair share ? Oil by Shutterstock <p> Myles Allen has argued that we do n't have the right to stop countries such as India from using its coal . He suggests instead making companies that use fossil fuels responsible for burying an equal amount of carbon to reduce net emissions . <p> But there is also scope for appealing to the ideals of international cooperation . We should be optimistic in light of the above psychological research about the capacity of the human race to put the long-term needs of the many above the short-term needs of the few . Big decisions could be facilitated by many of the psychological processes we have described , that focus on global identity , long-term gain rather than short-term loss , intergroup competition and reputation , rewards , shared norms , providing sufficient and clear information , and instilling trust and transparency .

This sounds like a low bar . @@8677910 <p> Can you explain the concept of the Anthropocene and its importance for understanding the current climate crisis ? <p> Anthropocene is the proposed name for the present stage of Earth history : a time in which human activity is transforming the entire planet in unprecedented and dangerous ways . Scientists divide Earth 's 4.5 billion year history into time intervals that correspond to major changes in the conditions and forms of life on Earth . <p> The Pleistocene Epoch , which began about 2.5 million years ago , was marked by what are commonly known as ice ages . The glaciers finally retreated about 11,000 years ago , initiating what geologists call the Holocene Epoch , characterised by a relatively stable and warm climate . Holocene conditions made agriculture possible , and that in turn laid the basis for the rise and spread of human civilisations . As Johan Rockstr ? m of the Stockholm Resilience Centre says , Holocene conditions are the only ones that we know for sure are compatible with complex human societies . <p> In the 1980s a growing number of scientists became @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and specific ecosystems ; that some changes were affecting the world as a whole . Examples included radioactive fallout from nuclear bomb tests , damage to the ozone layer caused by widely-used chemicals , and global climate change caused by greenhouse gas emissions . These concerns led to the launch of the largest and most complex programme of international scientific cooperation ever undertaken -- the International Geophysical-Biophysical Programme , which coordinated the efforts of thousands of scientists around the world from 1990 to 2015 . <p> The IGBP 's work produced a huge leap forward in scientific understanding of the Earth System -- including disturbing confirmation that human activity is not just disrupting that system , but doing so in ways that are more extensive and fundamental than anyone had imagined . In 2000 , at an IGBP meeting to review its first decade of research , the Nobel Prize winning chemist Paul Crutzen argued convincingly that defining features of the Holocene no longer exist -- that the Earth had entered a new epoch . He suggested the name Anthropocene , from the Greek word anthropos , meaning human being . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ is a much more complete understanding of the global carbon cycle and its relation to climate change . Scientists have known since the 1800s that carbon dioxide in the atmosphere regulates the global temperature by allowing solar energy to reach Earth as light , while restricting the reflection of heat back into space . If there was a lot more carbon dioxide in the air , Earth would be like Venus -- too hot to support life . If there was far less , Earth would be like Mars -- too cold for life . But while it was known by the 1960s that atmospheric carbon dioxide was increasing , scientists did n't know if the increase was unusual , and if so , how out of the ordinary it was , and what its effects might be . <p> Thanks to studies coordinated by the IGBP , we now know that for at least 800,000 years , atmospheric carbon dioxide has varied within a strictly limited range -- never lower than 180 parts per million in cold times , never higher than 300 ppm in warm times . Over very @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the oceans , keeping Earth 's temperatures within surprisingly well-defined limits . Now , as a direct result of fossil fuel combustion , the concentration is over 400 ppm , and it is growing fast . Human activity has disrupted a complex natural cycle that took millions of years to evolve and stabilise , and that disruption is rapidly changing the state of the planet . <p> As Crutzen and Will Steffen wrote , " Earth is currently operating in a no-analogue state . In terms of key environmental parameters , the Earth System has recently moved well outside the range of natural variability exhibited over at least the last half million years . The nature of changes now occurring simultaneously in the Earth System , their magnitudes and rates of change , are unprecedented and unsustainable . " <p> You say in your book that climate change is usually seen as a gradual process , but that the reality can be very different . Can you explain what this means ? <p> Science has long known that conditions on Earth have changed over time -- that much of the planet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ areas that are now cold were once tropical -- but it was believed that such shifts took place very slowly , over thousands of years or longer . One of the most surprising results of recent research into past climate is that rapid climate change has been the rule , not the exception . The climate is remarkably sensitive to quite small changes in the atmosphere and oceans , and rather than gradually warming or cooling , it has tended to lurch from one state to another , in years or decades rather than millennia . As one prominent scientist puts it , Earth 's climate is an ornery beast that violently overreacts even to small nudges . <p> That 's particularly relevant today , when greenhouse gas concentrations are not only high , but are rising more quickly than ever before . That puts unprecedented stress on the climate system , greatly increasing the possibility of runaway climate change , of a relatively quick shift into a completely different climate regime . That could mean , for example , that what we experience today as extreme but rare heat waves @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tipping point , ecosystems wo n't have time to adjust , species wo n't have time to evolve , and human societies might not have time to adapt . Climate tipping points , by their nature , are impossible to predict : depending on the speed of change , we might not even know we 've passed one until well after the point of no return . <p> That adds urgency to the crisis . We do n't know how long we have before climate change goes from dangerous to extremely dangerous , but we know that continuing with business as usual makes such a shift increasingly likely . What we do in this century , and probably in the next few decades , will determine the kind of world our grandchildren will inherit . <p> You focus on the Second World War as the point at which global environmental change takes off . Why was this ? <p> When Crutzen recognised that we are in a transition to a new epoch , he suggested that the Anthropocene may have begun at the time of the Industrial Revolution . That was @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Anthropocene , fossil capitalism was born in the 1800s , when factories and railroads and ships began burning coal on a massive basis . An economic and social system that must grow or die became dependent on fossil carbon to power its growth , and the history of capitalism since then has been marked by its ever-increasing use of coal , gas and oil . <p> That change began in the Industrial Revolution , but when scientists at the IGBP undertook the detailed work of quantifying the changes in the Earth System that define the Anthropocene , they discovered an unexpected pattern . In almost every case , graphs of long-term trends in the Earth System ( atmospheric carbon dioxide , ozone depletion , species extinctions , loss of forests , and so on ) show gradual growth from 1750 to about 1950 , when a steep increase began . From 1950 to the present the trend lines have gone almost straight up . " <p> More and more scientific research has confirmed that conclusion , and now most scientists involved in Anthropocene research argue that while the dependence on fossil fuels began with the Industrial Revolution , the new epoch actually began in the second half of the 20th century . They 've dubbed the period since 1950 the Great Acceleration . <p> One of the principal things I 've tried to do in Facing the Anthropocene is to explain the social and economic forces that drove this hockey-stick pattern . Why did n't growth and environmental destruction continue increasing gradually ? Or , to put it another way , why did all the trends suddenly accelerate together ? When I studied long-term trends in fossil capitalism , including the growth of fossil production and use , the automobilisation of Western society , corporate concentration and the rise of monopolies , the mass introduction of synthetic petrochemical-based products , the industrialisation of agriculture , and more , I found that the Second World War played a key role in accelerating every single one . <p> Mainstream economists and historians typically treat wars as @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . That 's been a consistent theme of Anthropocene research -- the most recent update to the Great Acceleration statistics , published in 2015 , says that it has been almost entirely driven by a small fraction of the human population . That 's not to say that their social analysis @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the right track , and it is shocking that some left critics fail to recognise that . <p> Second , making such criticisms central to our response builds walls between scientists and the left , when what we should be doing is engaging with scientists , contributing our views and analysis to the global discussion . We need to seize this remarkable opportunity to unite the latest scientific findings with an ecological Marxist analysis in a socio-ecological account of the origins , nature and direction of the crisis . If the left stays out of the discussion , if we condemn it from the sidelines , we will be leaving Anthropocene science and scientists under the ideological sway of neoliberalism , and we will be irrelevant to the most important scientific development of our time . <p> In the 1980s , in the face of resistance from chemical companies , the world banned gases that were destroying the ozone layer . The ozone layer in the upper atmosphere is a vital part of Earth 's life support system -- it literally makes life possible by blocking deadly ultraviolet radiation .
